summary: What the character screen says about each pack item (user 2026-09-27: "the stats should highlight what they do ... like walnut and strawberry"): its tag (the kind of thing) and one line of what it is. The figures (food, healing, damage, burn, what it builds) are worked out from the game's own data by ItemInfo (scripts/ui/inventory/item_info.gd), not written here. An optional 'history' (the climbing gear, user 2026-09-29: 'give quick history lessons of that item and where and how it was used') follows the line on the screen; standard historiography (basis H: verify before quoting), and it says so where the game invents.

musket.text: A smoothbore flintlock: slow to load, heavy ball, deadly at fifty paces.

over_under.text: Two barrels, one over the other: a second shot before the long reload.

bow.text: A self bow of one stave: quiet and quick to shoot again.

pistol.text: A horse pistol: one shot, close in.

spear_pair.text: Two light spears carried on the back, thrown by hand.

tomahawk.text: A trade hatchet, thrown or kept in the hand.

atlatl.text: The long arm that sends a dart farther and harder than a hand can.

dart_bundle.text: Long darts for the atlatl, tied in a bundle for the back.

quiver.text: A leather quiver on a shoulder strap, for the arrows.

powder_horn.text: A cow's horn of priming powder, hung at the side.

torch.text: A split of fat pine that burns bright and long.

felling_axe.text: An American felling axe, the frontier's first tool.

mattock.text: A pick on one side, a grubbing blade on the other.

hoe.text: A broad iron blade on a straight haft: breaks ground for a bed and keeps the weeds down.

digging_stick.text: A hardwood stick, its point hardened in the fire: breaks ground slowly where there is no hoe.

seed_corn.text: Flint corn kept back from the harvest: a few kernels to a hill.

seed_beans.text: Dry beans kept for sowing: they climb the corn.

seed_squash.text: Squash seed: the vines shade the ground between the hills.

seed_tobacco.text: Tobacco seed, fine as dust: set out in a well-worked bed.

seed_flax.text: Flaxseed: sown thick for the fibre.

corn.text: An ear of flint corn: roast it on a fire, or pound it into meal at the stone.

roast_corn.text: An ear roasted in its husk.

charred_corn.text: An ear left too long in the coals.

beans.text: A pound of dry beans: boil them on a fire.

bean_pot.text: A pot of beans boiled soft.

scorched_beans.text: Beans boiled dry and caught on the pot.

squash.text: A squash: roast it on a fire. It keeps for weeks.

roast_squash.text: Squash roasted soft in the ashes.

charred_squash.text: Squash burnt black on one side.

tobacco_leaves.text: Green tobacco leaves: cure and twist them at the workbench into tobacco for the pipe.

flax.text: Pulled flax stalks: the fibre makes cord at the workbench.

skinning_knife.text: A short, stout blade for skinning and butchering game.

fire_steel.text: A striker of steel: struck on flint, it throws sparks into tinder.

log.text: An eight-foot length of trunk, bucked from a felled tree.

firewood.text: A bundle of limbs and split top wood.

branches.text: Small limbs and twigs: kindling, brush and boughs.

pole.text: A sapling trimmed straight: rafters, rails, a lean-to.

stone.text: Fieldstone for a hearth, a chimney or a fire ring.

flint.text: A nodule of chert that strikes fire on steel.

venison.text: Fresh game meat, deer or buffalo, a meal's worth.

deer_hide.text: Green from the knife: the tanning frame scrapes it into rawhide or dresses it into buckskin.

bison_robe.text: A buffalo's winter coat, green from the knife and still in its wool: dressed with the hair on, the warmest robe a man can sleep in.

tallow.text: Hard white fat rendered from a buffalo: candles, soap, and grease for leather and a gunlock.

tongue.text: The buffalo's tongue, the plains hunters' delicacy and the first cut they take.

antler.text: Tines for handles, flakers and buttons.

wolf_pelt.text: A thick grey winter coat, green from the knife: stretch it on a hoop before it slips.

fox_pelt.text: A red fox's pelt, a staple of the fur trade.

blackberries.text: From the brambles at the woods' edge, in late summer.

strawberries.text: Small and sweet, from the open fields in June.

plantain.text: Broad leaves that grow where people walk; bruised, they are laid on wounds.

wintergreen.text: Teaberry: the leaves make a tea for aches and a cold.

ginseng.text: A scarce root of the shaded maple woods, bought dear at Albany.

acorns.text: The oaks' mast: bitter until leached.

hazelnuts.text: Picked in their husks from the hazel thickets, before the squirrels have them.

willow_bark.text: The inner bark of the black willow: steeped, the old remedy for fevers and aches.

yarrow.text: Soldier's woundwort: the leaves packed into a cut stop the bleeding.

elm_bark.text: Slippery elm's inner bark, slick when wet: boiled into a gruel that soothes the gut.

elderberries.text: Dark purple berries of the damp thickets, cooked down into a syrup for colds and chills.

hemp_tops.text: The resinous flowering tops of hemp run wild from the settlers' fields.

bearberry.text: Kinnikinnick leaves: dried, and smoked with red-osier bark and tobacco.

dogwood_bark.text: Red-osier's inner bark, scraped and dried: the red willow of kinnikinnick.

jimsonweed.text: Jamestown weed, rank and poisonous: soldiers who ate it at Jamestown went mad for eleven days.

crabapples.text: Small, hard and sour: better pressed for cider or dried than eaten.

jerky.text: Dried, salted meat that keeps for months.

cornmeal.text: Ground maize, for mush and johnnycake.

roast_venison.text: Venison roasted over the coals: safe to eat, a meal's worth.

charred_venison.text: Venison left too long on the fire, black outside.

small_game.text: A hare or a raccoon dressed from the trap line: roast it on the fire before it turns.

roast_small_game.text: Small game roasted over the coals: lean, and safe to eat.

charred_small_game.text: Small game left too long on the fire, black outside.

brook_trout.text: A speckled trout of the cold brooks and riffles, red-bellied in the fall. By the pound.

salmon.text: Lake salmon up the river on its fall run, silver and heavy. By the pound.

sucker.text: A bottom-feeding sucker of the pools, bony, but plenty in the spring run. By the pound.

perch.text: A barred yellow perch of the slow pools: small, sweet, easily caught. By the pound.

pike.text: A pike from the slow edges: long, toothed, good eating. By the pound.

eel.text: A river eel, taken at night: rich and fat. By the pound.

bullhead.text: A brown bullhead, the catfish of the muddy pools. By the pound.

sturgeon.text: Lake sturgeon come up to the rapids: a giant, pounds and pounds of it.

pickerel.text: A chain-marked pickerel of the weedy marsh. By the pound.

roast_fish.text: Fish roasted over the coals: safe to eat. By the pound.

charred_fish.text: Fish left too long on the fire: half of it is char.

johnnycake.text: Cornmeal baked in the ashes into two flat cakes.

burnt_johnnycake.text: Johnnycake burnt black in the ashes.

brains.text: Every animal has brains enough to tan its own hide: worked into a deer hide on the tanning frame.

buckskin.text: A hide dressed soft and smoked: for moccasins, leggings and shirts.

rawhide.text: Scraped and dried hard: lacing and lashings for snowshoes, repairs and frames.

plantain_salve.text: Plantain worked into a salve at the alchemy table: it draws and heals a wound.

wintergreen_tea.text: Teaberry leaves steeped hot: it warms you through and eases aches.

ginseng_tonic.text: A root sliced and steeped: it steadies a tired body.

willow_bark_tea.text: Willow bark steeped bitter: it brings a fever down and dulls the pain of wounds.

slippery_elm_gruel.text: Elm bark boiled to a slick gruel: it settles the flux and lets a sore gut keep its food.

elderberry_syrup.text: Elderberries cooked down thick: it drives a deep chill out of the bones.

sinew.text: The long back sinew of a deer, dried: split fine, it is the thread of moccasins and mitts.

fishing_rod.text: An ash rod with its line tied to the tip, a quill float and a hook: no reel, the rod does the work. Key 8 takes it out.

fish_spear.text: A pole with barbed points for fish seen in the shallows and at the weir. Key 8, twice.

shoots.text: Long straight shoots cut from an arrowwood thicket: peeled and straightened over the fire, arrow shafts.

pine_pitch.text: Amber resin scraped from a wounded pine: melted with charcoal, the glue for points and fletching; it makes a torch burn.

feathers.text: Wild turkey wing and tail feathers from under the oaks, split and trimmed for fletching arrows.

flint_knife.text: A chert blade knapped sharp and bound into a split handle: it skins, butchers and cuts as a belt knife does.

stone_axe.text: A chert head lashed into a split haft: it fells trees and cuts saplings as an axe does, slowly. Draw it with the axe key.

stone_pick.text: A long chert point lashed to a stout haft: it breaks rock and digs ore as a mattock does, slowly. Draw it with the tool key.

bog_iron.text: Rusty lumps of limonite dug from the wet hollows: smelted with charcoal in the forge's shaft, bar iron.

clay.text: Grey clay from a cut bank: it lines a smelting shaft and a forge's hearth, and seals a charcoal mound.

charcoal.text: Wood charred slowly under earth: the only fire hot enough to smelt iron and weld it.

bar_iron.text: A bar of wrought iron from the bloom, hammered out at the forge: the stuff of axes, knives, traps and tools.

gun_barrel.text: A smoothbore barrel welded round a mandrel and bored: with a lock and a stock at the workbench, a musket.

pistol_barrel.text: A short barrel for a pistol: with a lock and a stock at the workbench, a flintlock pistol.

gunlock.text: A flintlock: plate, cock, frizzen and springs forged and filed to fit. A flint in its jaws strikes the spark.

gunstock.text: A stock split from a log and carved: it takes a barrel and a lock at the workbench.

bone_awl.text: An antler tine ground to a fine point: it pierces buckskin for the sinew thread of moccasins, mitts and clothes.

bow_drill.text: A bow, a spindle and a hearth board: twirl it at a laid fire until a coal catches. It may take a few tries; a wet fire is harder.

cordage.text: Sinew twisted into cord: a length makes a snare, or a line for a rod.

stake_set.text: Two forked stakes, a trigger and a bait stick, cut for a deadfall: raccoon, marten and mink under a falling log.

steel_trap.text: A long-spring steel trap, bought from the traders: foxes, wolves and the water animals, set on the trail.

bar_lead.text: A pound of bar lead: melted at the fire and poured into the mould, sixteen musket balls.

bullet_mould.text: An iron scissor mould and a ladle, cut for your musket's ball.

hooks_line.text: Linen line on a winder, iron hooks and shot: a rod's line and hook, or a night line set from the bank.

dried_wolf_pelt.text: Stretched on a hoop and dried: a wolf's winter coat that keeps and trades, or sews into mitts.

dried_fox_pelt.text: Stretched on a hoop and dried: a red fox's coat that keeps and trades, or sews into mitts.

marten_pelt.text: A marten's pelt from the trap line, green from the knife: the trade's best small fur. Stretch it on a hoop.

mink_pelt.text: A mink's small dark pelt from a trap by the water, green from the knife: stretch it on a hoop.

fisher_pelt.text: A fisher's heavy dark pelt from the trap line, green from the knife: stretch it on a hoop.

raccoon_pelt.text: A raccoon's grizzled pelt with its ringed tail, green from the knife: stretch it on a hoop.

dried_marten_pelt.text: Stretched on a hoop and dried: a marten's rich brown fur that keeps and trades well.

dried_mink_pelt.text: Stretched on a hoop and dried: a mink's dark fur that keeps and trades.

dried_fisher_pelt.text: Stretched on a hoop and dried: a fisher's heavy fur that keeps and trades.

dried_raccoon_pelt.text: Stretched on a hoop and dried: a raccoon's coat that keeps and trades.

rum.text: West Indies rum by the gill, from a squat bottle of green glass.

tobacco.text: Cured leaf twisted into a rope, cut off by the pipeful.

clay_pipe.text: A long white clay pipe, the kind in every pocket from Albany to the Ohio.

whiskey.text: Monongahela rye by the gill, out of a square case bottle: strong, and it warms the throat.

cider.text: Hard cider from pressed crabapples, worked in the jug: a farm drink, slow to make a man merry.

sweet_cider.text: Crabapples fresh from the press: sweet, a little food, and in two days it turns hard.

laudanum.text: Tincture of opium by the drop: it stills pain and the flux, and it takes hold of a man like nothing else.

snuff.text: Tobacco dried and ground fine, taken by the pinch from a tin: no pipe, no fire.

chew.text: A quid of sweetened twist to keep in the cheek for hours.

kinnikinnick.text: The eastern woodlands' smoking mixture of bearberry leaves and red-osier bark, taken up by traders and hunters.

kinnikinnick_mix.text: Bearberry leaves and red-osier bark rubbed with a little tobacco: a pipe that goes further.

climbing_stakes_wood.text: Two fire-hardened stakes in the fists while you hold on: the grip tires a little slower (x0.85).
climbing_stakes_wood.history: Fire-hardening a wooden point is one of the oldest crafts: wooden spears preserved in European bogs and lake beds are hundreds of thousands of years old, and in 1765 trap stakes, tent pegs and digging sticks were still made this way. Honey hunters in Africa and Asia have long climbed tall trees by driving wooden pegs into the trunk and standing on them. Carrying stakes to climb with, as here, is this game's idea built on those old ways.

climbing_claws_wood.text: A hardwood copy of the Japanese ashiko (foot claws), teeth fire-hardened: hanging still costs x0.6. Old Pieter says the real ones are iron, and that a quiet man from the far East walks these ridges who could show you. Nobody has ever followed his tracks; he does not leave any.
climbing_claws_wood.history: Ashiko are Japanese foot claws: a plate strapped under the foot with iron teeth at the toe, worn with the hand claws called shuko or tekagi. They belong to the shinobi (ninja) traditions of the Sengoku and Edo periods, used for climbing walls and trees and for keeping a footing on slopes and beams. Most of what is told of them comes from later martial-arts schools and books, so the details are uncertain. The real ones were iron. This hardwood, fire-hardened pair is a copy made from knowledge handed down: in this game, the old hunter's tale of an iron pair a Dutch sailor brought home from Japan, where the Dutch East India Company's post at Dejima was Europe's one door from 1641 to 1854. The tale and the copy are the game's own.

climbing_stakes_bone.text: Two ground bone stakes: they bite deeper than wood, and the grip tires slower (x0.75).
climbing_stakes_bone.history: The cannon bones of a deer's legs were the Eastern Woodlands' standard stock for awls, needles and points: split with a wedge, then ground to shape on sandstone. Bone awls turn up at village sites across what is now New York, from long before contact to the 1700s. A pair of bone climbing stakes is this game's idea; the craft behind it is old and local.

climbing_claws_bone.text: A bone copy of the Japanese ashiko (foot claws), strapped on with buckskin: hanging still costs x0.5.
climbing_claws_bone.history: Ashiko are Japanese foot claws: a plate strapped under the foot with iron teeth at the toe, worn with the hand claws called shuko or tekagi. They belong to the shinobi (ninja) traditions of the Sengoku and Edo periods, used for climbing walls and trees and for keeping a footing on slopes and beams. Most of what is told of them comes from later martial-arts schools and books, so the details are uncertain. The real ones were iron. This split deer bone pair is a copy made from knowledge handed down: in this game, the old hunter's tale of an iron pair a Dutch sailor brought home from Japan, where the Dutch East India Company's post at Dejima was Europe's one door from 1641 to 1854. The tale and the copy are the game's own.

climbing_stakes_stone.text: Two flint-pointed stakes lashed with sinew: they bite into bark and cracks (x0.65).
climbing_stakes_stone.history: Chert and flint were knapped into points and blades in the Northeast for thousands of years, and Onondaga chert from central New York was carried far. By the 1760s many Native people used trade iron and brass instead, but knapping lived on, and the gunflint in every lock was knapped by hand in Europe. A point lashed into a split haft with sinew is how spears and knives were hafted; using it as a climbing stake is this game's idea.

climbing_claws_stone.text: A flint-toothed copy of the Japanese ashiko (foot claws), bound with sinew: hanging still costs x0.42.
climbing_claws_stone.history: Ashiko are Japanese foot claws: a plate strapped under the foot with iron teeth at the toe, worn with the hand claws called shuko or tekagi. They belong to the shinobi (ninja) traditions of the Sengoku and Edo periods, used for climbing walls and trees and for keeping a footing on slopes and beams. Most of what is told of them comes from later martial-arts schools and books, so the details are uncertain. The real ones were iron. This flint-toothed pair is a copy made from knowledge handed down: in this game, the old hunter's tale of an iron pair a Dutch sailor brought home from Japan, where the Dutch East India Company's post at Dejima was Europe's one door from 1641 to 1854. The tale and the copy are the game's own.

climbing_stakes_iron.text: Two forged iron spikes: the best bite there is, the grip tires at half the rate (x0.5).
climbing_stakes_iron.history: The colonial blacksmith forged spikes, nails, hinges and tools from bar iron bought from the furnaces. Iron spikes for climbing belong mostly to later mountaineering, but iron-spiked soles for ice are old: the Swiss scholar Josias Simler described them for crossing Alpine passes in 1574. Here a smith would make them to order.

climbing_claws_iron.text: Iron ashiko, the Japanese foot claws as they were really made: hanging still costs x0.35.
climbing_claws_iron.history: Ashiko are Japanese foot claws: a plate strapped under the foot with iron teeth at the toe, worn with the hand claws called shuko or tekagi. They belong to the shinobi (ninja) traditions of the Sengoku and Edo periods, used for climbing walls and trees and for keeping a footing on slopes and beams. Most of what is told of them comes from later martial-arts schools and books, so the details are uncertain. Iron is what the real ones were made of. A pair in the New York woods could only have come a long way: the Dutch East India Company's post at Dejima in Nagasaki was Europe's one door into Japan from 1641 to 1854, and Dutch families lived along the Hudson and the Mohawk. In this game the old hunter tells of such a pair; his copies in wood, bone and stone are how the knowledge came down.

canoe_stake.text: A stake cut and peeled from a pole. Driven into the gravel round a canoe's outline, they hold the building bed the bark is shaped on.

birch_bark_sheet.text: A whole sheet of white-birch bark peeled in one piece. Sewn and shaped over a bed of stakes it is the skin of a bark canoe, the tan inner bark turned out.

wattap.text: Roots of the pine and hemlock, dug up, split and soaked. Tough and supple, it is the thread a bark canoe is sewn with.

canoe_strip.text: A long strip split from a pole. Two on each side, pegged with the bark between them, make a canoe's gunwales.

canoe_rib.text: A thin rib split and shaved from a pole. Steamed until it bends, it is set under the gunwales to press the bark out to the canoe's curve.
